# waterqualityuganda

<!-- badges: start -->

[![License: CC BY
4.0](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-CC_BY_4.0-lightgrey.svg)](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)
[![R-CMD-check](https://github.com/openwashdata/waterqualityuganda/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/openwashdata/waterqualityuganda/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml)

<!-- badges: end -->

The goal of waterqualityuganda is to provide the data of a monthly
monitoring of drinking water quality along the chain from borehole
sources to household storage in four Ugandan districts (Nakaseke in
Central Region, Kaabong in Karamoja, Kumi in Teso and Luuka in Busoga),
collected between November 2024 and September 2025 by Whave Solutions
Limited.

For each borehole, water was sampled at the source and, in three
households using that borehole, from the container used to carry water
home (usually a jerrycan) and from the drinking water storage
container. Samples were analysed for *E. coli* by membrane filtration
of 100 mL and incubation for 18 to 24 hours. The aim of the monitoring
was to find out where contamination occurs: at the source, during
transport or during storage.

## Installation

You can install the development version of waterqualityuganda from
[GitHub](https://github.com/) with:

``` r
# install.packages("devtools")
devtools::install_github("openwashdata/waterqualityuganda")
```

```{r}
## Run the following code in console if you don't have the packages
## install.packages(c("dplyr", "knitr", "readr", "stringr", "gt", "kableExtra"))
library(dplyr)
library(knitr)
library(readr)
library(stringr)
library(gt)
library(kableExtra)
```

Alternatively, you can download the individual datasets as a CSV or XLSX
file from the table below.

1.  Click Download CSV. A window opens that displays the CSV in
    your browser.
2.  Right-click anywhere inside the window and select "Save Page As...".
3.  Save the file in a folder of your choice.

```{r, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

extdata_path <- "https://github.com/openwashdata/waterqualityuganda/raw/main/inst/extdata/"

read_csv("data-raw/dictionary.csv") |>
  distinct(file_name) |>
  dplyr::mutate(file_name = str_remove(file_name, ".rda")) |>
  dplyr::rename(dataset = file_name) |>
  mutate(
    CSV = paste0("[Download CSV](", extdata_path, dataset, ".csv)"),
    XLSX = paste0("[Download XLSX](", extdata_path, dataset, ".xlsx)")
  ) |>
  knitr::kable()

```

## Data

The package provides access to four datasets, one per observational
unit:

-   `borehole_visits`: one row per field visit to a borehole source.
-   `household_visits`: one row per field visit to a household, with
    the containers and water handling practices of that household.
-   `samples`: one row per water sample (bottle), with its laboratory
    result.
-   `labblanks`: one row per laboratory blank, the sterile-water
    control run alongside the samples.

`samples$visit_id` links each sample to the visit it was collected at.
The two visit tables share one id space, so a `visit_id` occurs in
exactly one of them: in `borehole_visits` for samples of type
`borehole` and `borehole_duplicate`, and in `household_visits` for
samples of type `transport_container` and `storage_container`.

```{r}
library(waterqualityuganda)
```

### borehole_visits

The dataset `borehole_visits` contains the location of each visited
borehole and a community member's remarks on the taste, smell and
colour of its water. It has `r nrow(borehole_visits)` observations and
`r ncol(borehole_visits)` variables.

```{r}
borehole_visits |>
  head(3) |>
  gt::gt() |>
  gt::as_raw_html()
```

For an overview of the variable names, see the following table.

```{r echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
readr::read_csv("data-raw/dictionary.csv") |>
  dplyr::filter(file_name == "borehole_visits.rda") |>
  dplyr::select(variable_name:description) |>
  knitr::kable() |>
  kableExtra::kable_styling("striped") |>
  kableExtra::scroll_box(height = "200px")
```

### household_visits

The dataset `household_visits` contains, for each visited household,
the borehole it collects water from, the types of transport and
storage container, how long water stays in the transport container,
whether the household boils its drinking water and how often and how
it cleans both containers. It has `r nrow(household_visits)`
observations and `r ncol(household_visits)` variables.

```{r}
household_visits |>
  head(3) |>
  gt::gt() |>
  gt::as_raw_html()
```

For an overview of the variable names, see the following table.

```{r echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
readr::read_csv("data-raw/dictionary.csv") |>
  dplyr::filter(file_name == "household_visits.rda") |>
  dplyr::select(variable_name:description) |>
  knitr::kable() |>
  kableExtra::kable_styling("striped") |>
  kableExtra::scroll_box(height = "200px")
```

### samples

The dataset `samples` contains one row per bottle of water: where and
when it was collected, what it was taken from, and the *E. coli* count
of the laboratory analysis together with the derived contamination
category. It has `r nrow(samples)` observations and `r ncol(samples)`
variables.

```{r}
samples |>
  head(3) |>
  gt::gt() |>
  gt::as_raw_html()
```

For an overview of the variable names, see the following table.

```{r echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
readr::read_csv("data-raw/dictionary.csv") |>
  dplyr::filter(file_name == "samples.rda") |>
  dplyr::select(variable_name:description) |>
  knitr::kable() |>
  kableExtra::kable_styling("striped") |>
  kableExtra::scroll_box(height = "200px")
```

### labblanks

The dataset `labblanks` contains the laboratory blanks: sterile water
filtered and incubated in the same laboratory session as the field
samples, to detect contamination introduced by the laboratory
procedure itself. It has `r nrow(labblanks)` observations and
`r ncol(labblanks)` variables.

```{r}
labblanks |>
  head(3) |>
  gt::gt() |>
  gt::as_raw_html()
```

For an overview of the variable names, see the following table.

```{r echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
readr::read_csv("data-raw/dictionary.csv") |>
  dplyr::filter(file_name == "labblanks.rda") |>
  dplyr::select(variable_name:description) |>
  knitr::kable() |>
  kableExtra::kable_styling("striped") |>
  kableExtra::scroll_box(height = "200px")
```

## Example

Where along the chain from source to cup does drinking water become
contaminated? The plot below shows, for each type of sample, the share
of analysed samples in each contamination category. Borehole water is
mostly safe or slightly contaminated, while the majority of samples
from transport and storage containers are unsafe.

```{r contamination-by-sample-type, fig.height=4.5}
library(waterqualityuganda)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

sample_type_labels <- c(
  borehole = "Borehole",
  transport_container = "Transport container",
  storage_container = "Storage container"
)

samples |>
  filter(sample_type %in% names(sample_type_labels),
         !is.na(contamination_category)) |>
  count(sample_type, contamination_category) |>
  mutate(sample_type = factor(sample_type_labels[sample_type],
                              levels = rev(sample_type_labels))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = sample_type, fill = contamination_category)) +
  geom_col(position = position_fill(reverse = TRUE), colour = "white",
           linewidth = 0.6, width = 0.7) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(),
                     expand = expansion(0)) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("#c6dbef", "#9ecae1", "#6baed6", "#3182bd", "#08519c")
  ) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 2)) +
  labs(x = "Share of analysed samples", y = NULL,
       fill = "Contamination category",
       title = "E. coli contamination by sample type",
       subtitle = "Four districts in Uganda, November 2024 to September 2025") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "bottom",
        legend.title.position = "top")
```

To relate results to household practices, join `samples` to
`household_visits` on `visit_id`. For example, the share of unsafe
storage-container samples by whether the household boils its drinking
water:

```{r}
samples |>
  filter(sample_type == "storage_container",
         !is.na(contamination_category)) |>
  left_join(household_visits, by = "visit_id") |>
  group_by(boils_water) |>
  summarise(
    n_samples = n(),
    share_unsafe = mean(contamination_category == "Unsafe")
  )
```

## Notes on the data

-   **Matching of field and laboratory records.** The field survey and
    the laboratory survey were linked on district, date and bottle
    number. Bottle numbers restart every sampling day, and the same
    number was sometimes used twice on one day. Records were linked only
    when the key was unique on both sides; the column `match_status` in
    `samples` reports the outcome for every row, and rows that could not
    be linked are kept with missing values on the other side.
-   **Counts above 100.** The laboratory was instructed to record 101
    colonies when a plate had more than 100 colonies (too numerous to
    count). A few counts above 101 were recorded as typed. The logical
    column `tntc` marks all counts above 100; treat `ecoli_cfu` as
    censored for those rows.
-   **District names.** The laboratory form used the spellings
    "Kaboong" and "Kamuli" for the districts recorded as "Kaabong" and
    "Luuka" in the field survey. The field survey spelling is used
    throughout.
-   **Dropped rows.** Submissions before 1 November 2024 (pilot visits
    without region or survey type) and four laboratory results that were
    submitted twice were dropped.
